Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The Alder Street Volunteer Help Desk runs from a converted storefront near the bus depot. On weekday evenings, a rotating group of volunteers answers messages from residents who need help finding food deliveries, rides to appointments, translation, or a place to ask a follow-up question. The team’s shared inbox labels each incoming message before a coordinator decides who should take it. The volunteers are not professional dispatchers, and the inbox label is meant to help them sort work rather than promise that a request has been resolved.

Mara, who coordinates the Tuesday shift, said, “People sometimes write ‘urgent’ because they are worried, and sometimes because they need an answer before the pharmacy closes. We still have to read the whole message.” In the team’s normal workflow, the label is only one signal; a coordinator can look at the details and contact the sender. The code included below is the only routing logic the team has supplied for this review. There is no accompanying description of how messages are collected, how the age field is assigned, or whether another part of the inbox changes a label later.

During a recent evening shift, volunteers saw several kinds of requests arrive close together. One message asked whether a grocery box could be delivered the next morning. Another asked for a ride to a clinic, and a third asked for help reading a notice written in English. A fourth sender wrote that a bus had been missed and asked whether anyone could call back. These examples help explain the setting, but the notes do not say what values any of those messages had in the system fields used by the function.

The shared inbox displays message details in a panel beside the label, so volunteers can read the sender’s wording after the label appears. On a busy shift, a coordinator may scan the label first and then open the message. Luis, a volunteer who covers the late desk, described one handoff this way: “The label caught my eye, but I checked the message before I told the next person what to do.” The group wants a review that distinguishes what the function itself decides from what people may do afterward.

Here is the complete function supplied for the review:

def route_message(message):
    if message.get('urgent') and message.get('age', 0) < 42:
        return 'priority'
    return 'standard'

The notes do not define the meaning of the number 42, the unit for age, or the expected type of the urgent field. They also do not specify whether a missing field is common, whether a message can be edited after submission, or whether the function is called once or more than once. Treat those details as unknown rather than filling them in from assumptions about help desks or messaging software.

   - Volunteers cover the inbox in blocks, and the person who first sees a message may not be the person who follows up.

They remembered the topics and the order in which they noticed them, but they did not retain the underlying field values, so none of those recollections can establish how this function would label a particular real message.

For a useful review, explain the visible decision rule in ordinary language and describe the role of the fallback values and returned labels only to the extent that the supplied code supports it. When discussing possible tests, use examples that can be expressed from the function’s inputs and outputs; do not claim that a test result has already been observed. The team is especially interested in understanding the conditional relationship in the code, not in receiving a proposed replacement implementation.

The Thursday coordinator, Ben, added, “We can decide what to do with a label after we understand exactly what created it.” The desk is keeping the same shared inbox during the next volunteer cycle, and the coordinators will continue reading the message text alongside its label.
